opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a really interesting question, and honestly one I think about a lot, because it's easy to conflate the two when you're just using a product like ChatGPT or Claude day to day.

The way I tend to think about it is that there are roughly two layers. There's the model itself: the pre-training, the data quality, the post-training with things like supervised fine-tuning, preference tuning, and more recently the reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards that gives us these reasoning models. Then there's everything wrapped around it at inference time: tool calling, web search, code execution, retrieval, memory, the system prompt, and the orchestration logic that decides when to call which tool.

From the user's perspective it all blends into "the assistant got better." But if you look at it more carefully, a lot of the practical improvement, especially on things like factual accuracy and up-to-date information, comes from tooling. A model that can search the web or run a Python interpreter doesn't need to memorize every fact or do arithmetic in its head. That reduces hallucinations quite a bit, and it's not because the weights got smarter, it's because the model is offloading what it's bad at to something that's good at it.

That said, I don't think you can fully separate them, because using tools well is itself a model capability. The model has to learn when to call a tool, how to formulate a good query, how to interpret the results, and when to ignore a bad search result. That's trained in during post-training. So if you put a weaker model in the same harness, you often don't get the same benefit. The tooling raises the ceiling, but the model determines how close you get to that ceiling.

One way I like to reason about it, and this is also how I approach it when I'm building things from scratch, is with ablations. You take the same model with and without tools on the same benchmark, or you take different models in the same harness. That gives you a rough sense of where the gains come from. In my experience, for knowledge-heavy or math-heavy tasks, tools give you a big jump. For things like reasoning through an ambiguous problem, writing, or understanding what the user actually wants, that's still very much the model.

I'd also say there's a bit of a shift happening. A few years ago the story was mostly "scale the model." Now a lot of the progress is in inference-time scaling, letting the model think longer, use tools, verify its own outputs. So the line between "model" and "system" is getting blurrier, and I think that's actually a healthy development, because it means we're not relying only on ever-bigger training runs to make these systems more useful.

r002.rationale: The response says tooling contributes substantially to some practical improvements, especially factual accuracy and up-to-date information. It does not state that many current LLM use cases center on the tooling wrapped around the model.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and honestly it's one I think about a lot, because it's genuinely hard to disentangle the two. If you look at what people experience when they use something like a coding assistant today versus two years ago, a big part of that improvement is the model, but I'd argue an underappreciated part is everything wrapped around the model.

So let me try to break it down a bit. On the model side, we've seen real gains: better pretraining data, longer context windows, more reasoning-oriented post-training, better instruction following. Those are things you can measure on benchmarks, and they're real. A model from 2026 is just more capable on a fixed prompt than a model from 2023.

But then there's the tooling layer, and that's things like tool use, retrieval, agentic loops where the model can run code and look at the output and iterate, structured outputs, system prompts that encode a lot of domain knowledge. And what's interesting is that a lot of that doesn't require a better model, it requires a smarter harness around the model. If you take an older model and give it the ability to execute code and read the error message, it becomes dramatically more useful for coding than the same model just generating text in one shot. That's not the model getting smarter, that's the system getting smarter.

The way I try to separate them, at least in my own experiments, is to hold one constant. So you take the same model, and you compare raw prompting versus the full agentic setup with tools and retrieval. And then separately you take the same harness and swap in an older and a newer model. And what I usually find is that both matter, but they matter for different things. The tooling gives you reliability and grounding, so fewer hallucinations, more up-to-date information, the ability to verify. The model gives you the ceiling on reasoning quality, how well it handles ambiguous or novel problems.

And there's a feedback loop, too, which makes it even harder to disentangle. Newer models are specifically trained to use tools well, so part of the "model improvement" is really the model being optimized for the tooling. So the distinction gets blurry.

If I had to put a rough number on it, for everyday tasks, I'd say the tooling and scaffolding probably accounts for more of the perceived quality jump than people assume. But for the hard tail, the problems where you really need good reasoning, that's still mostly the model. And I think for practitioners the practical takeaway is: before you reach for a bigger model, make sure you've actually exhausted what better tooling and better context can give you. It's often cheaper and more controllable.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to separate the model from the system around it. The model contributes things like how well it understands your question, follows instructions, and reasons through a problem. The tooling determines what information and actions it has access to. Can it retrieve a document, run code, or check its answer against something?

And those interact. A calculator can give you an exact result, but the model still has to recognize when to use it, provide the right inputs, and interpret the output. So better tooling can make the same model much more useful, and a better model can make the same tools more effective.

If you want to distinguish the contributions, you really need controlled comparisons. Keep the model fixed and change the tools, then keep the tools fixed and change the model. Looking only at the final assistant experience, it’s very difficult to attribute an improvement to one or the other. You’re experiencing the quality of the whole system.

r001.rationale: The response says better tooling can improve a model’s usefulness, but does not propose that a leading commercial interface paired with the best open-weight LLM could achieve nearly the same practical quality.

r002.rationale: The response explains that tooling affects access to information and actions, but does not state that many current LLM use cases center on tooling wrapped around the model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it helps to separate the model’s capability from the capability of the whole system. When you use an AI assistant, you’re usually interacting with more than a language model. There might be web search, retrieval over documents, a code interpreter, and some logic that decides which tool to call.

For example, if an assistant answers a question about something that happened yesterday, that doesn’t necessarily mean the model itself has become more knowledgeable. It may have retrieved the right information. Similarly, getting a numerical answer right with a Python tool is different from getting it right through the model alone. Both are useful, but they tell us different things.

To distinguish those contributions, I would hold one part fixed. Compare two models with the same tools and instructions, and then compare the same model with and without those tools. You also want to look at the intermediate steps: Did it find the right document? Did it recognize that it needed a calculation? Did it interpret the result correctly?

And there’s an interaction here. Better models can be better at using tools—knowing when to call them, supplying the right arguments, and recovering when something fails. So I wouldn’t attribute the improvement entirely to one side. For the user, the quality of the complete assistant matters. But if we want to understand where progress is coming from, we need to evaluate those components separately.
